title: The lost sheep and the lost coin (Luke 15:1–10)
hookLine: a shepherd leaves ninety-nine and a woman sweeps the whole house

cards: You've lost your keys, and you're already late. You check your pockets, then your bag, then your pockets again. You lift the couch cushions.
You retrace every step. You are not calm, and you are not reasonable, and you are not going anywhere until you find them.

Luke fifteen opens with tax collectors and sinners crowding close to hear Jesus, and some Pharisees and scribes grumbling about it. In the Douay-Rheims: "This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them."
So Jesus answers with three stories about losing something. Today, the first two: a sheep, and a coin.

teach.b: First, a shepherd with a hundred sheep. One wanders off. He leaves the ninety-nine in the wilderness and goes after the lost one until he finds it.
On paper, it isn't sensible. Ninety-nine out of a hundred is a fine result. But the shepherd isn't counting that way.
And when he finds it, he doesn't scold it or drag it home.
He puts it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and calls his friends: "Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost."
Early Christians painted that image, a shepherd with a sheep across his shoulders, on the walls of the catacombs in Rome. Then a woman with ten silver coins, drachmas in Luke's Greek, loses one.
She lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house, searching carefully until she finds it. And she calls her friends and neighbors: rejoice with me.
Look at who the seekers are: a shepherd out in the wilderness, and a woman sweeping her floor. Christians read them both as pictures of God.
Each story ends the same way: there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. Not polite approval. A party.
And notice who does the work. The sheep doesn't find its way home. The coin can't do anything at all.
The searching belongs to the one who lost them.

how: Catholics hear Luke 15 at Sunday Mass and often in Lent; the Good Shepherd carrying a sheep is painted on the walls of the Roman catacombs.

games.why: he goes after it until he finds it, carries it home on his shoulders, and throws a party: rejoice with me.

practice: Think about the people who used to be close and aren't anymore: a friend who stopped showing up, a cousin you haven't heard from, someone who stepped away from church, or from the group, or from everybody.
Without asking whose fault it was, let one face come, and hold them gently for a minute. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: groat. The old Douay-Rheims word for the coin: one of ten a woman lost, then swept her house to find.

orig.note: Greek: a silver coin. The woman had ten and lost one; the Douay-Rheims calls it a groat.

carryVoice: Your line: he goes looking. And there is joy in heaven over the one he finds. That's day forty-six.
